results.title: Fermat polygonal number theorem

results.title: Grundman's bound on consecutive Niven numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $b \ge 2$ and $a \ge 1$ be integers. Then for some $i$ with $0 \le i \le 2b$, the integer $a + i$ is not divisible by the sum of its base-$b$ digits. Equivalently, the $2b + 1$ consecutive integers $a, a + 1, \dots, a + 2b$ are not all $b$-Niven numbers, where a $b$-Niven number is a positive integer divisible by the sum of its base-$b$ digits.

results.summary: Write $\mathrm{mex}(s)$ for the least positive integer not in a finite set $s$ of natural numbers. If $m$ is a positive integer with $m \notin s$, then $\mathrm{mex}(s) \le m$.

results.title: First summands of the anti-Tribonacci construction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \ge 1$, $A_n$ is the first entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction: $A_1 = 1$, and for $n \ge 2$, $A_n$ is the least positive integer that is not among the values $A_k$, $B_k$, $C_k$, $D_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $A_0 = A_1 = 1$.

results.title: Second summands of the anti-Tribonacci construction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \ge 1$, $B_n$ is the second entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction: $B_1 = 2$, and for $n \ge 2$, $B_n$ is the second smallest positive integer that is not among the values $A_k$, $B_k$, $C_k$, $D_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $B_0 = B_1 = 2$.

results.title: Third summands of the anti-Tribonacci construction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \ge 1$, $C_n$ is the third entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction: $C_1 = 3$, and for $n \ge 2$, $C_n$ is the third smallest positive integer that is not among the values $A_k$, $B_k$, $C_k$, $D_k$ with $1 \le k < n$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $C_0 = C_1 = 3$.

results.title: Anti-Tribonacci numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \ge 1$, the anti-Tribonacci number $D_n$ (OEIS A265389) is the fourth entry of the $n$-th quadruple $(A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n)$ of the anti-Tribonacci construction, so $D_n = A_n + B_n + C_n$ and $D_1 = 6$. At $n = 0$ the definition gives $D_0 = D_1 = 6$.

results.title: First anti-Tribonacci numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Writing $D_n$ for the $n$-th anti-Tribonacci number, the first four anti-Tribonacci numbers are $D_1 = 6$, $D_2 = 16$, $D_3 = 27$ and $D_4 = 36$.

results.title: Members of a greedy $3$-subsumfree sequence below a bound
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ (the source takes $x < y < z$), let $S_{x,y,z}$ consist of $x$, $y$, $z$ and every natural number $n > z$ that is not a sum $a + b + c$ of members $a < b < c$ of $S_{x,y,z}$ smaller than $n$. This definition gives, for each natural number $m$, the finite set of members of $S_{x,y,z}$ below $m$.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ and $d$ be natural numbers. results.title: Unsums of upper Wythoff numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A positive integer $p$ is an *upper Wythoff number* when the letter at index $p - 1$ (indices start at $0$) of the infinite Fibonacci word $0100101001001\ldots$ is $1$; that is, the upper Wythoff numbers are the positions of the letter $1$ in the Fibonacci word counted from one. A positive integer $x$ is an *unsum* (OEIS A260317) if there are no upper Wythoff numbers $p < q$ with $p + q = x$.

results.title: The upper Wythoff numbers below 30
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The positive integers $p < 30$ such that the letter at index $p - 1$ (indices start at $0$) of the infinite Fibonacci word is $1$, that is, the upper Wythoff numbers below $30$, are exactly $2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23, 26, 28$.

results.title: The unsums up to 21
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The unsums (OEIS A260317) that are at most $21$ are exactly $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 19, 21$.

results.title: Gaps between unsums
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be the unsums (OEIS A260317): the positive integers that are not a sum $p + q$ of upper Wythoff numbers $p < q$. For $i \ge 0$, the $i$-th gap between consecutive unsums (counted from zero) is $a_{i+2} - a_{i+1}$; this is OEIS A260311 shifted by one.

results.title: The first thirteen gaps between unsums
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be the unsums (OEIS A260317) and let $g_i = a_{i+2} - a_{i+1}$ for $i \ge 0$. Then the gaps $g_0, g_1, \dots, g_{12}$ are $1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2$.

results.title: Markers among the unsum gaps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A natural number $i$ is a *marker* if $i \ge 10$ and the $i$-th gap between consecutive unsums of upper Wythoff numbers (counted from zero) equals $2$.

results.title: Markers in the gaps between unsums
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Call a gap index $i$ a marker if $i \ge 10$ and the $i$-th gap between consecutive unsums (counted from zero) equals $2$. For $j \ge 0$, the $j$-th marker is the $j$-th marker in increasing order, counted from zero, so the $0$-th marker is the smallest one.

results.title: Words between markers in the unsum gap sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $g_0, g_1, g_2, \ldots$ be the gaps between consecutive unsums, and call an index $i \ge 10$ with $g_i = 2$ a marker. Let $m_0 < m_1 < m_2 < \cdots$ be the markers in increasing order. For each $j$, the $j$-th word between markers is $g_{m_j + 1} g_{m_j + 2} \cdots g_{m_{j+1} - 1}$, the word of the gaps strictly between the $j$-th and the $(j+1)$-th marker.

results.title: The words $W_i$ of the unsum gap sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $i \ge 1$, the word $W_i$ is the word of gaps strictly between the $(2i-2)$-th and $(2i-1)$-th markers of the unsum gap sequence, with markers counted from zero; for $i = 0$ the definition gives the same word as for $i = 1$.

results.title: The first two markers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Call a gap index $i$ a marker if $i \ge 10$ and the $i$-th gap between consecutive unsums (counted from zero) equals $2$. The smallest marker is $10$ and the second smallest is $12$.

results.title: The first palindrome
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g_k$ be the $k$-th gap between consecutive unsums (OEIS A260317), counted from zero, and let $m_0 < m_1 < \cdots$ be the markers, the indices $k \ge 10$ with $g_k = 2$, in increasing order. The word $W_1$ of the gaps $g_k$ with $m_0 < k < m_1$, in increasing order of $k$, consists of the single digit $3$.

results.title: The last gap of size one between unsums
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ be the unsums (OEIS A260317), and for $i \ge 0$ let $g_i = a_{i+2} - a_{i+1}$ be the $i$-th gap between consecutive unsums, counted from zero. Then $g_9 = 1$, and $g_i \ne 1$ for every $i \ge 10$.

results.title: Digit sums between markers are two less than Fibonacci numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $j$, the digit sum of the $j$-th word between markers of the unsum gap sequence, plus $2$, is a Fibonacci number: it equals $F_m$ for some natural number $m$.

results.title: Digit sums of the words between markers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci numbers, with $F_0 = 0$ and $F_1 = 1$. For every $j$ (words counted from zero), the digit sum of the $j$-th word between markers of the unsum gap sequence, plus $2$, equals $F_{\lfloor j/2 \rfloor + 5}$.

results.title: The gap words are palindromes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g_k$ be the $k$-th gap between consecutive unsums (OEIS A260317), counted from zero, and let $m_0 < m_1 < \cdots$ be the markers, the indices $k \ge 10$ with $g_k = 2$, in increasing order. For $i \ge 1$ let $W_i$ be the word of the gaps $g_k$ with $m_{2i-2} < k < m_{2i-1}$, in increasing order of $k$. Then for every $i \ge 1$, the word $W_i$ read backwards is $W_i$ itself.

results.title: The palindromes begin and end with the digit 3
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $g_k$ be the $k$-th gap between consecutive unsums (OEIS A260317), counted from zero, and let $m_0 < m_1 < \cdots$ be the markers, the indices $k \ge 10$ with $g_k = 2$, in increasing order. For $i \ge 1$ let $W_i$ be the word of the gaps $g_k$ with $m_{2i-2} < k < m_{2i-1}$, in increasing order of $k$. Then for every $i \ge 1$, the word $W_i$ is nonempty, its first digit is $3$, and its last digit is $3$.

results.title: A word $3V3$ between markers is followed by a word starting with $3V$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ be a finite word of natural numbers, and suppose that the $j$-th word between markers of the unsum gap sequence is $3V3$. Then $3V$ is a prefix of the $(j+1)$-th word between markers, and if the $(j+1)$-th word has the same digit sum as the $j$-th word, then the two words are equal.

results.title: Length of the period-doubling iterates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the word obtained by applying the period-doubling substitution $1 \mapsto 10$, $0 \mapsto 11$ to the one-letter word $1$ a total of $n$ times has length $2^n$.

results.title: Letters of the period-doubling iterates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w_m$ be the word obtained by applying the period-doubling substitution $1 \mapsto 10$, $0 \mapsto 11$ to the one-letter word $1$ a total of $m$ times. For all natural numbers $m$ and $k$ with $k < 2^m$, the letter of $w_m$ at index $k$ (indices start at $0$) equals the letter of the period-doubling word at index $k$.

results.title: First letters of the period-doubling word

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k > 1$, let $A_n$ be the anti-recurrence numbers of the linear form $(1, \dots, 1)$ of length $k$, and put $i = \lfloor k/2 \rfloor$ and $\kappa = k^2 + 1$. results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ be a linear form with positive integer coefficients, of trace $\tau = a_1 + \dots + a_k$, and let $A_1$ be its first anti-recurrence number. results.title: Cost of an insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count $n$ and capacity $m$, and let $x$ be an item. Inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT costs $1 + n$ if $m > 0$ and $n = m$, and costs $1$ otherwise.

results.title: Amortized cost of dynamic-table insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a dynamic table $T$ with item count $n$ and capacity (number of slots) $m$, let $\Phi(T) = 2n - m$, an integer that may be negative. If inserting an item $x$ into $T$ has cost $c$ and returns the table $T'$, then $c + \Phi(T') - \Phi(T) \le 3$. Here the cost of an insertion is one unit for writing $x$ plus one unit for each old slot copied when a full table is doubled.

results.title: Slots after an insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ and item count $n$, let $x$ be an item, and let $T'$ be the table returned by inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT, with capacity $m'$. Then the slots of $T'$ are $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$, followed by a slot holding $x$, followed by $m' - (n + 1)$ empty slots.

results.title: Insertion preserves well-formedness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $T$ is a well-formed dynamic table and $x$ is an item, then the table returned by inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT is well formed.

results.title: Insertion appends to the contents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $T$ is a well-formed dynamic table and $x$ is an item, then the contents of the table obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ are the contents of $T$ followed by $x$.

results.title: Repeated insertion preserves well-formedness of a dynamic table
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Call a dynamic table with item count $n$ well formed when, for every slot index $i$, slot $i$ is occupied exactly when $i < n$. If a dynamic table $T$ is well formed, then for every array $xs$, the table obtained from $T$ by inserting the entries of $xs$ one at a time with TABLE-INSERT, in array order, is again well formed.

results.title: Inserting an array appends it to the contents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $T$ is a well-formed dynamic table and $x_1, \dots, x_k$ is an array of items, then inserting $x_1, \dots, x_k$ into $T$ one at a time, in this order, gives a table whose contents are the contents of $T$ followed by $x_1, \dots, x_k$.

results.title: Capacity after inserting into the empty table
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Starting from the empty dynamic table and inserting the items of an array of length $k$ one at a time, the resulting table has capacity (number of slots) at most $2k$.

results.title: Total cost of insertions into the empty table
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Starting from the empty dynamic table and inserting the items of an array of length $k$ one at a time, the total cost is at most $3k$, where each insertion costs one unit for writing the new item plus one unit for each old slot copied when a full table is doubled.

results.title: Strict cost bound for nonempty insertion sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Starting from the empty dynamic table and inserting the items of a nonempty array of length $k$ one at a time, the total cost is less than $3k$.

results.title: Lookup in a dynamic table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$, each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. The lookup at logical position $i$ returns the item held by $s_i$ when $i < n$ and $s_i$ is occupied; it returns no value when $i < n$ and $s_i$ is empty, and when $i \ge n$.

results.title: Lookup beyond the item count returns nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count $n$. For every natural number $i \ge n$, the lookup at logical position $i$ in $T$ returns no value.

results.title: Lookup succeeds exactly below the item count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table holding $n$ items. For every natural number $i$, the lookup at logical position $i$ in $T$ returns a value if and only if $i < n$.

results.title: Deletion from a dynamic table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$, each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. Deleting the last item of $T$ gives the following table. If $n = 0$, the result is $T$ itself. Otherwise, if $4(n-1) < m$, that is, the load factor after deletion is strictly below $1/4$, the table contracts: the result has slots $s_0, \dots, s_{n-2}$ followed by $\lfloor m/2 \rfloor - (n-1)$ empty…

results.title: Item count after deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Applying deletion to a dynamic table with item count $n$ gives a table with item count $n - 1$ when $n \ge 1$, and item count $0$ when $n = 0$.

results.title: Capacity after deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with capacity $m$ and item count $n$, and apply deletion to $T$. If $n = 0$, the capacity stays $m$. If $n \ge 1$ and $4(n-1) < m$, the new capacity is $\lfloor m/2 \rfloor$. Otherwise the capacity stays $m$.

results.title: Slots after deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ holding $n \ge 1$ items, and let $m'$ be the capacity of the table obtained by applying deletion to $T$. The slots of that table are the first $n - 1$ slots $s_0, \dots, s_{n-2}$ of $T$ followed by $m' - (n - 1)$ empty slots.

results.title: Deletion preserves well-formedness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table, that is, its occupied slots are exactly its first $n$ slots, where $n$ is its item count. Then the table obtained by applying deletion to $T$ is again well-formed.

results.title: Deletion removes the last item from the contents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table. The contents of the table obtained by applying deletion to $T$ is the contents of $T$ with its last entry removed; when the contents of $T$ is empty, it stays empty.

results.title: Deletion preserves lookups below the last position
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table holding $n$ items, and let $i$ be a natural number with $i < n - 1$. After applying deletion to $T$, the lookup at logical position $i$ returns the same result as the lookup at position $i$ in $T$.

results.title: Lookup at the vacated position after deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count $n$, where $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$. After applying deletion to $T$, the lookup at logical position $n - 1$ returns no value.

results.title: Cost of initializing the transitive-closure matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Boolean adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices, the staged transitive-closure computation with no pivot stages (only the initialization of the $n \times n$ matrix) charges exactly $n^2$ time units, one for each cell assignment.

results.title: Cost of one transition stage

results.title: Running time of the transitive-closure algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Boolean adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices, the transitive-closure algorithm charges exactly $n^2 + n^3$ time units: $n^2$ cell assignments to initialize the matrix and $n^2$ in each of the $n$ transition stages.

results.title: Cost of transitive closure on the empty graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For the graph with no vertices, the transitive-closure algorithm charges $0$ time units: it performs no cell assignments.

results.title: Cost of transitive closure on one vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Boolean adjacency matrix on a single vertex, the transitive-closure algorithm charges exactly $2$ time units: one cell assignment for the initialization and one for the single transition stage.

results.title: Greedy algorithm on a matroid
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an oracle $O$ that accepts or rejects each finite subset of a type $\alpha$ and a list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the greedy algorithm starts from the empty set, processes the elements of $L$ in order, adds an element $e$ to the current set $T$ when $O$ accepts $T \cup \{e\}$ and leaves $T$ unchanged otherwise, and returns the final set. It charges one unit of time per element processed.

results.title: Running time of the greedy scan
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every oracle $O$ on finite subsets of a type $\alpha$, every finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ and every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the greedy scan with oracle $O$ from $S$ over $L$ takes time exactly the length of $L$.

results.title: Running time of the matroid greedy algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every oracle $O$ on finite subsets of a type $\alpha$ and every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the greedy algorithm with oracle $O$ on $L$ takes time exactly the length of $L$, one oracle query per element.

results.title: The greedy scan over a concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every oracle $O$ on finite subsets of a type $\alpha$, every finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ and all lists $P$ and $Q$ of elements of $\alpha$, the set returned by the greedy scan with oracle $O$ from $S$ over $P$ followed by $Q$ equals the set returned by the greedy scan with oracle $O$ over $Q$ starting from the set that the scan with oracle $O$ from $S$ over $P$ returns.

results.title: The matroid greedy result is independent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a matroid on a type $\alpha$ and let $O$ be an oracle that accepts a finite set $A \subseteq \alpha$ exactly when $A$ is independent in $M$. For every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the set returned by the greedy algorithm with oracle $O$ on $L$ is independent in $M$, and each of its elements occurs in $L$.

results.title: The matroid greedy result is a base
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a matroid on a type $\alpha$ with ground set $E$, and let $O$ be an oracle that accepts a finite set $A \subseteq \alpha$ exactly when $A$ is independent in $M$. For every list $L$ in which an element of $\alpha$ occurs if and only if it lies in $E$, the set returned by the greedy algorithm with oracle $O$ on $L$ is a base of $M$.

results.title: Independence system
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A predicate $\mathrm{indep}$ on the finite subsets of a type $\alpha$ is an independence system when the empty set is independent and every subset of an independent set is independent.

results.title: A scan inside an independent set keeps everything
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type, let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$ and let $I$ be an independent set. For every list $L$ of elements of $I$ and every finite set $S \subseteq I$, the greedy scan of $L$ starting from $S$ returns $S$ together with all elements of $L$.

results.title: A scan that accepts nothing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type, let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence oracle on the finite subsets of $\alpha$, let $S$ be a finite subset of $\alpha$ and let $L$ be a list of elements of $\alpha$ such that $\mathrm{indep}$ rejects $S \cup \{e\}$ for every $e$ in $L$. Then the greedy scan of $L$ starting from $S$ returns $S$.

results.title: Greedy optimality gives the augmentation axiom
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$ for which the greedy algorithm is optimal. If $I$ and $J$ are independent sets with $|I| < |J|$, then some element $e \in J$ with $e \notin I$ makes $I \cup \{e\}$ independent.

results.title: Greedy-optimal independence systems are matroids
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$ for which the greedy algorithm is optimal. Then there is a matroid $M$ on $\alpha$ whose ground set is all of $\alpha$ such that a finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ is independent in $M$ exactly when $S$ is independent under $\mathrm{indep}$.

results.title: Rado–Edmonds theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$. The greedy algorithm is optimal for $\mathrm{indep}$ if and only if there is a matroid $M$ on $\alpha$ whose ground set is all of $\alpha$ such that a finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ is independent in $M$ exactly when $S$ is independent under $\mathrm{indep}$.
